quoted.text: Daishin Securities CSPs and AI labs: CSPs and AI labs had requested the development of lower-stack HBM products, such as 4-high and 6-high configurations, for use in low-end inference products. Those plans now appear to have been shelved, with 8-high once again emerging as the minimum stack height. NVIDIA: Rubin’s specifications have changed amid base die supply constraints and requests from customers prioritizing bandwidth over cost efficiency. The original plan called for a mix of 8-high and 12-high HBM, but the 8-high option appears to have been dropped. For Rubin Ultra, scheduled for release in 2027, multiple architectural variants are currently undergoing tape-out. Initial versions are expected to use the highest-specification 8-high HBM4, while subsequent versions are expected to adopt either 8-high or 12-high HBM4E. AMD: AMD is expected to use a mix of 8-high and 12-high HBM4 in its 2027 products. One notable development is the upcoming MI450, which is expected to increase the number of HBM stacks within the CoWoS package to 12, delivering 288GB of HBM4. The increase from eight to 12 HBM stacks per CoWoS package is a positive development for HBM content over the medium to long term. OpenAI and Anthropic: OpenAI is expected to adopt 12-high HBM4, while Anthropic is expected to use 8-high HBM4.

tweets.text:
I built 𝚌𝚙𝚞-𝚌𝚑𝚊𝚝, a reproduction of @openai's findings of covert communication using the CPU.

It runs on a generic host with 2+ Firecracker microVMs with no internet access. Works on x86 and even my M5 chip.

I was able to chat via 3 separate mechanisms:
① CPU contention
② Cache eviction timing
③ DRAM bandwidth contention 

… across multiple CPUs, defeating all Firecracker's production recommendations (no SMT, no KSM, tenants pinned to different cores.)

Essentially, if shared hardware is involved, there's a good chance your agents can communicate covertly. And with really decent latency.

The good news: this is decidedly different from a *side-channel attack* where the agents could steal information (Meltdown/Spectre), a category of attack that providers like Vercel Sandbox mitigate. Further, in our real-world environment, these 'whispering' techniques are much harder to pull off and easier for us to monitor and detect (sampling hardware counters + lots of at-scale statistical data.)

Noteworthy: ironically, OpenAI and Anthropic's models refused to do this work. Open weight models got the job done. I'm worried the labs' stance might backfire and get in the way of helping developers build correct and secure systems. e.g: building a secure sandbox requires having this kind of analysis, and without it, we'll have a less secure world.

I oddly love the models' engineering vernacular: gate, evidence, culprit, durable, provenance, contract…

A lot of these stem from most engineering being debugging and understanding existing systems, where you take on the detective / auditor roles. You do forensics.

I wonder what the *minimum viable English* in fact is to be productive. ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English contains ~900 approved words. I suspect we need far fewer.
